title: Disagreeing with love
hook: streams disagree on practice, conversion and marriage, and still share one people

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: shared ethics: giving, kindness and justice, from texts the streams read together. You heard these and these on day two hundred eighty-two. Today it goes to work, on the harder half: what happens when the streams don't agree.

Two schools of teachers, the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel, disagree. Not once: over and over, on law after law. In the Talmud's telling, each house insisted the law followed them, and the argument would not end. Then a voice came from heaven and settled it. But listen to how. The voice did not say one side was right and the other wrong. It said something stranger, and the rabbis kept the sentence.
screen: `SHAMMAI AND HILLEL.` → `A VOICE FROM HEAVEN.` → `NOT RIGHT AND WRONG.`

segments.voice: Disagreeing with love. Four turns. First, the voice. In the Talmud's telling, it said: these and these are the words of the living God, and the law follows the House of Hillel. Both views are words of the living God; one still becomes the practice. Second, why Hillel. The Talmud asks that itself, and answers: Hillel's students were gentle and humble. They taught Shammai's view along with their own, and even said Shammai's first. They won the law by the way they held the argument. Third, the test. The Mishnah says a dispute for the sake of heaven will last, and one that isn't, won't. Its example of the first kind is Hillel and Shammai. Its example of the second is Korah and his company, who rose against Moses for power. The question isn't whether people argue. It's what the argument is for. Fourth, the families. The two houses disagreed even about laws of marriage, which could have split them into two peoples. Yet the Talmud reports they did not refrain from marrying into each other's families. Today the streams disagree on real things: how to keep Shabbat, how a person converts, whose conversion counts, which marriages a rabbi will perform. Those disputes can wound, and love doesn't mean pretending they don't matter. The old model offers something narrower and harder: say the other side's view first, say it well, and keep the families at one table.
screen: `THESE AND THESE.` · `HILLEL: GENTLE, HUMBLE, OTHER VIEW FIRST.` · `A DISPUTE FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN.` · `THEY STILL MARRIED EACH OTHER.` · then, large: `DISAGREE WITH LOVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you disagree with about something that matters; not your worst fight, just one you can carry for two minutes. Do what Hillel's students did: say their view first, silently, in its strongest and fairest form, then say your own just as fairly, and notice whether anything softens. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer before you let them go.
Disagreeing with love. Holding a real dispute for the sake of heaven: stating the other view first and fairly, and staying one family. Today's word.
Your line: disagree with love. The other side's view, said first and said well. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish study is built on recorded disagreement: the Talmud preserves minority views beside the law, and study partners are expected to argue hard while learning each other's reasoning.

chat.says: Why did the law follow Hillel and not Shammai, if both were words of God?
options: The Talmud says Hillel's students were gentle and taught Shammai's view first.
Because the voice said Shammai's words weren't from God at all.
Because Hillel's house wrote its rulings down and Shammai's never did.
chat.meaning: In Eruvin, the Talmud says Hillel's students were gentle and humble, and taught Shammai's view along with their own, even first.

Shammai.meaning: a sage whose house argued law with Hillel's

Hillel.meaning: a sage whose gentle house the law follows

notes: Eruvin 13b paraphrased: bat kol, 'elu va'elu divrei Elohim chayim, and the halakha follows Beit Hillel'; reasons given (gentle, humble, taught Shammai's words and mentioned them first). The Talmud's mention of the dispute's duration was deliberately left out.
Avot 5:17 numbering varies between editions (5:17 or 5:20); confirm reference.
Yevamot 14b: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not refrain from marrying from one another despite disputes touching marriage law; confirm summary.
